name: Backbone Ridge

pitch_detail.notes: From the top of the 4th-class approach ledges, climb the low-angle white corner to the ridge crest, then follow the crest up to a stance at the foot of the obvious offwidth. Belay on the ledge below the wide crack.

The crux offwidth, straight up. The lower half takes small and hand-sized cams; the upper half protects only with a very large cam (BD #6), bumped along as you go. Some parties get by with a #5 and runout. Packs make it much harder, so haul or hang them. Expect a strenuous, knee-and-ankle-scraping struggle. Belay on hand-sized gear above.

Walk left from the belay and climb a long, blocky open-book corner toward a small roof. Short of the roof, step right and build the belay. Protection is good in the corner cracks; small cams and offset nuts are useful at the anchor.

Climb a low-angle finger crack just left of the crest; when it widens, step left into a wide-hands layback. From the top of the layback, trend left through cracks and blocks to the sharp ridgeline. The move off the finger crack is the pitch's crux and relies on small edges or smears.

Step down and left from the sharp ridge onto a large ledge, then scramble back to the crest and follow it to a small saddle below the Fin. The rock is lichen-covered and loose in places, with several possible lines; most parties simul-climb this section, keeping to the left side of the ridge where the choice is unclear. Watch rope drag and loose blocks.
Take the ramp up toward the base of the Fin headwall, crossing a gravel apron, and belay on a left-leaning ledge below the twin cracks. Easy ground, but gravel on the ledges makes it slick underfoot.

The first Fin pitch: climb the twin cracks and face holds above the ledge to a large flat ledge. Gear spacing is reasonable; a grassy crack to the right is an alternative but dirtier. Loose blocks sit on the ledge at the top, so place a high directional to keep the rope from pulling them onto the second.

The hardest Fin pitch: a tricky hand and finger crack around the left corner of the arête, then a right-facing corner to a semi-hanging stance straddling the Fin crest below a large roof. Superb rock in an exposed position. Ledge-fall potential low on the pitch; protect it well. The belay takes #1–#3 cams.

Climb the blocky crack a short way, then traverse right along horizontal cracks across the face of the Fin: a long, rising, near-horizontal shuffle past the roof with poor feet, few holds and very exposed. Gear is sparse in the middle, so protect well for the second as well as the leader. Some rock near the end of the traverse is questionable. Belay at the notch between gendarmes.

Easy but loose terrain along ledges and gravelly gullies toward the summit; most parties simul-climb or short-rope it. Choose flake anchors carefully and manage drag around the small walls. Near the top, a gravel apron and a shallow gully lead up and left to the summit, or contour left sooner to join the descent trail.

rappel_detail.notes: This is the sound half of the pair: even parties who then refused to continue down the line rated this first anchor good. It sits near 47.479°N, 120.832°W, which is a low-precision fix roughly 100 m east-north-east of the summit — enough to put you on the right ledge system, not to find the anchor itself.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed station on rock, marked by a cairn
rappel_detail.hazards: Loose rock throughout this descent — check the anchor before you commit to it.
rappel_detail.station: A short scramble east along the ledges below the summit, marked by a cairn. Parties report it easy to find, and reachable after only mellow scrambling.

rappel_detail.notes: A doubled 60 m rope only just reaches the ledge below; parties report finishing on the very ends of the rope, and a 70 m gives margin. From that ledge, go left, hug the wall and scramble and downclimb until the standard descent line is regained.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung tat on the wall, with a rock horn beside it as the alternative
rappel_detail.hazards: The second rappel runs directly over a loose flake big enough to kill, and the standard walking descent passes below — make sure nobody is underneath before the first person goes down.
rappel_detail.station: The lower station has been found as a tat anchor on the wall with a rock horn beside it — carry tat and a spare biner and judge it on the day. If neither is one you want to use, it is possible to climb back up to the upper station.

rappels: 2 rappels (~30m) from a cairned station used in icy conditions in lieu of the walk-off
descent_text: Most parties descend the east ledges and sandy summit gully toward Aasgard Pass and down to Colchuck Lake. When the upper descent gully is icy (common late season), rappel instead — two rappels on a 70m rope (60m works) using rock anchors to avoid the ice slope, with a documented rappel station near 47.479°N, 120.832°W. Watch for loose rock and verify anchor integrity on any rappel here — parties have found the anchors below the first station poor enough to turn round and downclimb instead, and the second rappel runs directly over a loose flake big enough to kill, with the standard walking descent passing below it.
approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Colchuck Lake Trail (~4 mi, 2,280 ft gain) → around the lake and up the moraine to the route base (roughly 200 ft left of Serpentine Arête); initial bushwhacking on brushy ledges until the party cliffs out and traverses up/right toward the ridge crest.
overview: A long, left-trending granite ridge line up the lower-right side of Dragontail's north face, mixing clean crack-and-corner pitches with looser scrambling, capped by the striking 'Fin' feature near the summit.
beta: After 4th-class scrambling to the first technical pitches, the route climbs an easy 5.8 pitch into the crux 5.9 offwidth (needs a #6 Camalot), then two more 5.8 pitches and a simul-climbing section to the base of the Fin. The Fin itself offers three spectacular pitches — an enjoyable 5.8 off the main ledge, a longer/harder pitch to a semi-hanging stance, then a single, almost-horizontal crack requiring 20+ meters of exposed, holds-poor traversing. Two mellow but loose pitches and more simul-climbing lead to the summit.
gear: aluminum crampons and light ice axe (early season)
fa: FA 1970 — M. Weigelt and J. Bonneville (Fin Direct variation 1975 — P. Cruver and K. Lewis).
face: North face, lower right side (ridge left of the white slabs), trending to the summit
